_meta.purpose: Banned-phrase lint for the Trenton, Missouri directory. Merged from Team A (A3 §6.1, §6.4) and Team B (B3 §5.1, §A.6) per RULINGS §2 gate 7.
_meta.matching: Each `pattern` is a regular expression, matched CASE-INSENSITIVELY against rendered page text (visible text nodes only, after templating). Regex metacharacters are escaped where a literal is intended.
_meta.override: A `fail` may be cleared only by moving the text into `quoted_attributed[]` with a visible source attribution on the page. Reviewer sign-off is recorded in the page front matter. There is no override for `warn` other than a written justification in the same field.

banned.why: Empty travel-blog filler. It describes no place in particular and survives being pasted onto any other town.
A placeholder standing in for a location we should simply name. If we know where it is, write the street or the landmark; if we don't, say we don't.

Unverifiable popularity and ranking claims dressed as description. We have visited nothing, measured nothing, and assembled no comparison set — and 'best-kept secret' is self-refuting on a public directory page.
The single most common adjective applied to small towns by writers who have not been there. Says nothing checkable.
Postcard adjectives about a place none of us has seen. 'Quaint' is condescending, and all three are sensory claims that ship only when they trace to a source or a photo we hold — we hold none.

Scale and activity inflation. A town this size does not bustle; 'vibrant' implies a scene where there may be a handful of businesses; 'thriving' is an economic claim we never measured and that is often false where an employer has closed.
Directory-speak for 'has', and it reliably precedes an unsourced claim. Use 'has' and cite it, or cut the sentence.
The definitional empty sentences. 'Something for everyone' is true of nowhere and informs no one; 'look no further' is sales patter asserting a completeness we do not have.

The audience-fanning opener, including the full 'whether you're a X or a Y' template. It invents reader personas to avoid committing to a fact, and pads the page instead of answering the question. No page may open this way.

History flavour with no dates. Where we hold a sourced date, print the date — the adjective is what you write when you don't — and 'step back in time' additionally treats a working town as a period exhibit.
Filler that names nothing being blended. Always replaceable by listing the actual things.
A claim about the character of real residents, made by people who have never met them. Not ours to make.
Regional stereotype substituted for reporting. Let the town be its own size by describing what is there, not how it supposedly feels.
Superlative sensory claims about scenery we have not seen. Nothing on this site is entitled to them.
A superlative sized entirely wrong for a town of a few thousand people, and unmeasurable anywhere.
Visitor hype: it instructs the reader's priorities and asserts visitor volume we have not measured. We say what a place is and let the reader decide whether to drive there.
Postcard vocabulary. Fails the portability test — it would read identically about any county seat in the Midwest.
Location filler used in place of an address, on a site whose whole premise is naming where things are.
Register mismatch and a well-known machine-writing tell. A neighbour answering a question does not use these words.
Reputation claims with no cited source. If a place is genuinely well known, cite who said so and when.

banned.pattern: \b(?:plenty of|no shortage of|an array of|a wide (?:range|variety) of|countless|endless|myriad|dozens of|hundreds of|scores of)\b
banned.why: Plural-of-abundance: quantity language with no count behind it. It implies supply we never counted and usually contradicts the real listing count printed on the same page. Where we hold a sourced count, print the number.
Fabricated social proof. We host no reviews and have interviewed nobody; this is an invented citation.
Asserts a reputation without naming who holds it. Either attribute it to a source or delete it.

banned.pattern: \byou(?:'|\u2019)?(?:ll| will) (?:find yourself|be amazed|love|discover)\b|\byou can(?:no|'|\u2019)?t help but\b|\bprepare to be\b|\bimagine (?:yourself|walking|strolling)\b
banned.why: Narrating the reader's experience and emotions. We do not know what they will find, and second-person fantasy is the loudest tell of generated travel copy.
The 'X isn't just Y, it's Z' construction. Rhetorical inflation carrying zero information.

banned.pattern: \bin conclusion\b|\ball in all\b|\bat the end of the day\b
banned.why: Summary padding. Pages end on their last useful fact and then the provenance block.
Abstract significance claims that cannot be sourced or falsified.

banned.pattern: \bin today(?:'|\u2019)?s [a-z-]+ world\b|\bwhen it comes to\b|\bit(?:'|\u2019)?s worth noting\b|\bnavigate the complexities\b
banned.why: Throat-clearing openers. The first sentence must carry information; these delay it.
Longevity claim without a founding date. If we have a sourced date, print the date instead of the adjective.
Asserts fieldwork we did not do. Nobody on this project opened a page, placed a call, or set foot in Grundy County.
The confirmation ceiling for this entire build is `unconfirmed` (RULINGS §1). No page may describe any field as verified.
Hours are the fastest-rotting and most harmful field on the site, and we hold no confirmed set for any entity. Phrased as reassurance, this sends someone on a drive to a locked door on our authority.
Intensified verification language. The stronger the assertion, the larger the lie, since the true count of confirmed records is zero.
Claims accuracy at a moment. We may say when we last looked at a source; we may never say the value was right when we looked.
We guarantee nothing, and a directory that guarantees anything about third-party businesses is misrepresenting its own position.
We are not official anything. Implying endorsement by the city, county, or Chamber is a false-affiliation claim.
Completeness overclaim. Every category page must instead state its real count and say plainly that it is not everything.
A coverage claim we can never support and that discourages exactly the owner submissions we depend on.
Maintenance overclaim. The only honest freshness signal is a stored last-checked date, never a promise.

banned.pattern: \b(?:open now|currently open|now open|still in business|open today|still operating)\b
banned.why: `status` defaults to unknown and several records are known closed or doubtful. Asserting present-tense trading is the failure mode this schema exists to prevent.

Generated business flattery and unsourced honours. This is the exact sentence a scraper writes when it knows only a name and a category, and 'award-winning' names neither the award nor the awarding body.
Superlative sized for a metropolis, applied to a rural county seat. Discredits the page instantly for any reader who lives there.
Quality superlatives with no measurable referent. Legal only inside an attributed quotation held in `quoted_attributed[]`.
Catches constructed superlatives ('largest X in the region') that need a number and a comparison set we do not have.
Vocabulary borrowed from places several orders of magnitude larger. The town has a downtown, not an urban core, and it has no suburbs and no metro — a resident spots this in one line.
'Scene' implies a critical mass of venues. Name the businesses we can actually list, and let the count speak.
Districts are a big-city planning concept. Using one here invents a geography of the town that does not exist.
Regional-importance claim with nothing behind it, and 'capital of' is routinely false in a way locals will catch.
An unsourced trend claim about a local economy. Frequently the reverse of the truth where an employer has closed.
Allowed only where a sourced date or a listing designation is printed in the same sentence. Otherwise it is decoration; justify or replace with the date.
Commonly true and commonly copied from an aggregator. Needs a first-party source or an owner submission; justify the source in review.
A popularity claim needs a cited measure. Permitted only when attributing a source's own words, with the attribution visible.
A cost claim that dates instantly and must be tied to a cited statistical source and its year, not asserted as a quality of the town.
Safety claims about a real community carry real consequences in both directions. Permitted only against a named, dated statistical source.
Evaluative adjectives about places and people we have not met. Counts against the adjective budget and needs a stated reason to survive review.
Sensory-provenance rule: every such description must trace to a source or a photograph we hold. We hold none, so the default outcome is deletion.
Usually a longer way of writing 'has', and it often smuggles in an entity we have not sourced. Justify or rewrite plainly.
An unsourced distance or travel-time claim. Distances ship only from a cited mapping or DOT source; 'just' also editorialises the effort.
Correct for the municipal government ('the City of Trenton'), wrong as a description of the place. Check which sense is meant; default to 'town'.
Generated business-description filler. Almost always deletable with no loss; justify if a source actually says it.
